signals.title: The winter timetable took 18% of the flights overhead. Freight held.
signals.metric_label: air freight across the timetable switch
signals.comparison: Low-cost and charter -30% · Full-service scheduled -16% · Business aviation -20% · Transatlantic passenger -24% · East Asia passenger -17% · All flights -18%
signals.interpretation: Airlines publish two timetables a year and switch on the last Sunday of March and of October. The move in passenger flying at that date is the calendar, not the economy, so it is shown once, here, and nothing else on this site is compared across it. A line that holds through the switch is flying because of demand rather than because of the timetable - which is why freight leads the board.
signals.caveat: Freight has a season of its own - the build-up to Christmas - so a flat line through late October is not a flat year. Only the same weeks a year earlier can separate that out, from 18 September 2027.
signals.sql:
SELECT day, carrier_kind, COUNT(*) AS flights
FROM flights
WHERE day BETWEEN '2026-09-27' AND '2026-11-21'
GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY 1, 3 DESC;

signals.title: Business aviation down 17% inside the winter 2026/27 schedule
signals.interpretation: Business jets, counted by airframe. Corporate and private travel at its most discretionary - the first line cut in a downturn and the first to return. Both windows are flown to the same timetable, so this is not the schedule switch - and it is larger than this line's usual week-to-week variation.
signals.caveat: The time of year is still in this figure: demand drifts inside a season too. It can only be taken out against the same weeks a year earlier, which begins 18 September 2027.
signals.sql:
SELECT day, COUNT(*) AS flights
FROM flights
WHERE is_bizav
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

signals.title: Freight keeps office hours
signals.comparison: 44.8 a weekday vs 26.5 at the weekend
signals.where: Mon 36 → Tue 56 → Wed 44 → Thu 44 → Fri 44 → Sat 25 → Sun 28
signals.interpretation: Freighters follow the working week of the businesses that load them, and the count climbs through it before easing on Friday. This is the closest thing overhead to a trade figure: it is capacity moving because somebody has goods to move.
signals.caveat: Cargo is attributed by operator, not by aircraft. A freighter flown by a passenger airline is not counted here, and belly freight under passengers is invisible to us entirely.
signals.sql:
SELECT dow, COUNT(*) AS freight_flights
FROM flights
WHERE carrier_kind = 'cargo'
  AND day BETWEEN '2026-11-19' AND '2026-11-25'
GROUP BY 1;

signals.title: Business jets keep the working week
signals.comparison: 245 business-jet flights a week · 3.3% of traffic
signals.interpretation: Counted by airframe, not by operator, so privately flown jets are included. The weekday tilt says most of this is work: meetings, site visits, deals. It is the most discretionary travel there is, which is what makes its level worth tracking.
signals.caveat: A business jet is identified by its type. Who is aboard and why is not observable, and some of this is private leisure.
signals.sql:
SELECT dow, COUNT(*) AS flights
FROM flights
WHERE is_bizav
GROUP BY 1;

signals.title: The working week barely changes how much flies - it changes what
signals.comparison: 1,026 flights a weekday vs 963 at the weekend
signals.interpretation: The total is almost flat, which is what you would expect over a point that mostly sees aircraft at cruise. Underneath it the mix moves hard in both directions: freight runs +69% on weekdays while charter runs +6%. Averaging a Tuesday with a Sunday cancels the two against each other and reports nothing. The composition is the signal; the count is not.
signals.caveat: This is the shape of one week, not a change in it. What moved, and against what, is on the macro board.
signals.sql:
SELECT daytype, carrier_kind, COUNT(*) AS flights
FROM flights
WHERE day BETWEEN '2026-11-19' AND '2026-11-25'
GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY 1, 3 DESC;

signals.title: 61% of the flights overhead neither start nor end in Denmark
signals.comparison: 49,701 pass through · 32,037 touch a Danish airport
signals.interpretation: Aarhus sits under the routings between Scandinavia and the Continent, and between Northern Europe and the rest of the world. Most of what the antenna hears is that corridor, not Danish demand - which is what makes the count usable as a signal about the wider network rather than one region.
signals.caveat: Only the 76% of flights with a verified or unverified route are counted here. Flights with no callsign, or a callsign not in the route tables, are not - and they are not assumed to be either kind.
signals.sql:
SELECT is_overflight, COUNT(*) AS flights
FROM flights WHERE origin IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1;

signals.title: Busiest city-pair overhead: Copenhagen – Aalborg
signals.interpretation: The busiest corridor is the one the record can measure most precisely. Week on week, this is the pair to watch for schedule changes first.
signals.caveat: A pair counts both directions. The balance between them is schedule shape, not demand asymmetry - a rotation is a rotation.

signals.title: Intercontinental routes crossing overhead
signals.interpretation: Long-haul flights pass over Denmark on the great circles between Central Europe and North America or Asia. Their presence is a reading on those corridors, not on Denmark.
signals.caveat: Distance is the great-circle length of the scheduled route, not the path flown.

signals.title: Traffic overhead runs north-east to south-west
signals.metric_label: of flights on the NE-SW axis
signals.interpretation: That axis is Scandinavia to the Continent. Direction is measured from the aircraft's own track, so it holds for every positioned flight - including the ones with no route.
signals.caveat: Eight compass sectors, from first to last position in range. A flight seen only briefly can land in the wrong sector.
signals.sql:
SELECT direction, COUNT(*) AS flights
FROM flights WHERE direction IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC;

signals.title: 50% of the freighters overhead are flown by Chinese cargo airlines
signals.comparison: 142 a week on China-Europe rotations · 20 freight operators · 3.4% of all traffic
signals.where: Air China Cargo, European Air Transport, China Cargo Airlines, ASL Airlines Belgium, China Southern Cargo
signals.interpretation: Freighters between China and the European cargo hubs - Liège, Brussels, Stansted, Billund - cross Denmark on the great circle, so one antenna in Aarhus hears a large share of that lane: e-commerce parcels westbound, machinery and luxury goods eastbound. The rest is the European overnight express network. Neither follows the passenger timetable.
signals.caveat: Cargo is attributed by operator, so only all-cargo airlines are counted. Freight in the hold of passenger aircraft - roughly half of air cargo worldwide - is invisible here, and a flight is not a tonnage: load factors are not observable.

signals.title: Flights to or from China crossing overhead
signals.interpretation: None of these land in Denmark. They are the Europe-China great circles that happen to cross this antenna's range, so the count is a reading on that corridor - and the split between the two directions is the same flow seen from both ends.
signals.caveat: Corridor routings shift with winds, airspace closures and slot times. Flights are not passengers or freight; a change here is a change in schedule before it is a change in demand.

signals.title: Flights to or from United States crossing overhead
signals.comparison: 3,478 bound for United States · 1,899 leaving it
signals.interpretation: None of these land in Denmark. They are the Europe-United States great circles that happen to cross this antenna's range, so the count is a reading on that corridor - and the split between the two directions is the same flow seen from both ends.
signals.caveat: Corridor routings shift with winds, airspace closures and slot times. Flights are not passengers or freight; a change here is a change in schedule before it is a change in demand.

signals.title: Wide-body share of traffic
signals.interpretation: Wide-body airframes indicate long-haul routings. Tracking this share separately from the flight count matters: the same number of flights carrying larger aircraft is more capacity, not flat activity.
signals.caveat: Airframe type is identified from the aircraft's registered type code. It does not tell us the cabin configuration or how full it is.
signals.sql:
SELECT ac_type, ac_desc, COUNT(*) AS flights
FROM flights
WHERE ac_type SIMILAR TO '(A33|A35|A38|B74|B77|B78).*'
GROUP BY 1,2 ORDER BY 3 DESC;

gauges.label: Air freight
gauges.reads: All-cargo operators. Freighters fly when there are goods to move, not when a timetable says so - the closest thing overhead to a trade figure.
gauges.sql:
SELECT day, COUNT(*) AS flights
FROM flights
WHERE is_cargo
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

gauges.label: China-Europe freighters
gauges.reads: Freighters flown by Chinese cargo airlines between China and European hubs: e-commerce parcels one way, machinery and luxury goods the other. A direct reading on one trade lane.
gauges.sql:
SELECT day, COUNT(*) AS flights
FROM flights
WHERE is_cargo AND carrier_country = 'CN'
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

gauges.label: Express and Western freighters
gauges.reads: DHL, UPS, FedEx and the European overnight parcel network, plus Western heavy freighters. Tracks parcel volumes and business-to-business shipping inside Europe.
gauges.sql:
SELECT day, COUNT(*) AS flights
FROM flights
WHERE is_cargo AND carrier_country <> 'CN'
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

gauges.label: Business aviation
gauges.reads: Business jets, counted by airframe. Corporate and private travel at its most discretionary - the first line cut in a downturn and the first to return.
gauges.sql:
SELECT day, COUNT(*) AS flights
FROM flights
WHERE is_bizav
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

gauges.label: Full-service scheduled
gauges.reads: Network airlines. Carries business travel and connecting traffic; less seasonal than holiday flying, but it follows the timetable.
gauges.sql:
SELECT day, COUNT(*) AS flights
FROM flights
WHERE carrier_kind = 'network'
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

gauges.label: Danish domestic
gauges.reads: Copenhagen to Jutland and back: shuttles that exist for the working week. Tracks Danish business activity more than tourism.
gauges.sql:
SELECT day, COUNT(*) AS flights
FROM flights
WHERE origin LIKE 'EK%' AND destination LIKE 'EK%'
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

gauges.label: Transatlantic passenger
gauges.reads: Passenger flights between Europe and North America crossing overhead. Long-haul capacity is expensive to fly empty, so it follows premium and tourist demand across the Atlantic.
gauges.sql:
SELECT day, COUNT(*) AS flights
FROM flights
WHERE far_region = 'North America' AND is_cargo IS NOT TRUE
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

gauges.label: East Asia passenger
gauges.reads: Passenger flights between Europe and China, Japan and Korea. Business ties and tourism with East Asia, and a reading on how open that corridor is.
gauges.sql:
SELECT day, COUNT(*) AS flights
FROM flights
WHERE far_region = 'East Asia' AND is_cargo IS NOT TRUE
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

gauges.label: Gulf hubs
gauges.reads: Flights to and from Dubai, Doha and the other Gulf hubs - the connecting route from Scandinavia to South Asia, Africa and Australia.
gauges.sql:
SELECT day, COUNT(*) AS flights
FROM flights
WHERE far_region = 'Gulf'
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

gauges.label: Low-cost and charter
gauges.reads: Price-led and holiday flying: household discretionary spending. The most seasonal line here, so it only means something year on year.
gauges.sql:
SELECT day, COUNT(*) AS flights
FROM flights
WHERE carrier_kind IN ('lowcost', 'leisure')
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

gauges.label: All flights
gauges.reads: Everything the antenna hears. Mostly the passenger timetable; shown as the yardstick the other lines are read against.
gauges.sql:
SELECT day, COUNT(*) AS flights
FROM flights
WHERE TRUE
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;
